jdso8u-d1e93-d1e103.summary: Editorial title (Wadding numbering, prologue question 2): whether the supernatural knowledge necessary for the wayfarer is sufficiently handed down in Sacred Scripture.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e117.summary: First argument for the negative: necessary knowledge was never lacking to the human race, but Scripture did not exist under the law of nature (Moses first wrote the Pentateuch), and under the Mosaic law only the Old Testament existed. So Scripture cannot be what supplies the necessary knowledge.
claims: Necessary knowledge was never lacking to humanity.
Scripture did not exist, or did not exist in full, under the law of nature and the Mosaic law.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e135.summary: Second argument for the negative: the more intelligent an author, the more he avoids superfluity, yet Scripture seems to contain superfluous material, such as ceremonies and many histories, whose knowledge is not needed for salvation.
claims: Wise authors avoid superfluity.
Scripture contains ceremonies and histories that seem unnecessary for salvation.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e157.summary: Third argument for the negative: for many acts Scripture does not settle with certainty whether they are mortal sins, though knowing this is necessary for salvation, since one who does not know an act is mortal sin will not adequately avoid it.
claims: Scripture leaves uncertain whether many acts are mortal sins.
Knowing which acts are mortal sins is necessary for salvation.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e184.summary: Argument for the affirmative from Augustine (City of God XI.3): canonical Scripture is what we believe about things we may not be ignorant of and cannot know by ourselves.
claims: Canonical Scripture provides what we need to know and cannot know by our own powers.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e208.summary: Scotus surveys the many heresies that reject all or part of Scripture: some reject it entirely; the Manichaeans reject the Old Testament as from an evil principle; Jews accept only the Old Testament; 'Saracens' (Muslims, described polemically) take something from both while adding much else; and various Christian heretics build on misread verses, e.g. Romans 14 or James 5, the latter leading some to hold that penance can be administered by non-priests.
claims: Many heresies reject all or part of Scripture.
Some heresies arise from isolated, misunderstood scriptural texts.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e280.summary: Scotus announces eight ways of rationally convincing all these opponents of Scripture's truth: prophetic prediction, the concord of the Scriptures, the authority of the writers, the diligence of those who received them, the reasonableness of their content, the unreasonableness of each error, the stability of the Church, and the clarity of miracles. This list structures the rest of the first part of his answer.
claims: Scripture's credibility can be rationally established in eight ways.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e312.summary: First way, prophecy: only God can naturally and with certainty foresee future contingents, so only he or one taught by him can predict them with certainty. Many such predictions in Scripture have been fulfilled, so there is no doubt the few that remain will follow (Gregory, Augustine).
claims: Only God, or one taught by God, can predict future contingents with certainty.
Many scriptural prophecies have been fulfilled.
This shows Scripture's divine origin and grounds trust in what remains unfulfilled.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e358.summary: Second way, concord of the Scriptures: many differently disposed people do not agree firmly and infallibly on things not evident from their terms or principles unless a higher cause inclines their intellects; the scriptural writers, differing and living in different times, fully agreed on such matters. Augustine illustrates this by contrast with the philosophers, but Scotus adds a reason: since only an evident object, or something virtually containing its evidence, can cause assent, and nothing but an intellect higher than ours can do so for non-evident matters, and only God can effectively teach humans, the agreement points to God as teacher.
claims: Diverse people agree firmly on non-evident matters only if a higher cause moves their intellects.
The scriptural authors agreed on such matters across different times.
Only God, as a higher intellect, can effectively teach humans non-evident truths.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e461.summary: Objection to the second way: later writers may simply have accepted their predecessors' teachings as disciples do, and so written nothing discordant, without God teaching them. Scotus notes that Augustine seems to answer this by observing that philosophers' disciples, though agreeing with their masters in some things, disagreed in others (Aristippus and Antisthenes, Aristotle and Plato).
claims: Agreement among later writers might be explained by their deference to earlier ones.
Philosophical disciples often contradicted their masters.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e518.summary: Scotus answers the question why later scriptural writers did not contradict earlier ones without a common teacher, in a way that partly concedes the objection: since the earlier writers handed on non-evident matters, later ones could not refute them by reason and, revering them as truthful masters, would not disbelieve them without a compelling argument. Philosophers could refute their masters because their subject allowed arguments from the terms; similarly a disciple historian does not contradict his master as a philosopher does, since past events are not evident.
claims: Non-evident teachings cannot be refuted by reason, so disciples tend not to contradict them.
Philosophical matters admit arguments from terms, which allows disciples to refute masters.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e575.summary: Rebuttal restoring the force of the argument: at least Ezekiel prophesying in Babylon and Jeremiah in Judea at the same time said much beyond what they received from Moses as common master, and on non-evident matters they could have disagreed unless they had a common teacher above the human intellect.
claims: Contemporary prophets independently agreed on non-evident matters beyond their common tradition.
This agreement requires a common teacher above human intellect.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e606.summary: Third way, authority of the writers: if the books are by their attributed authors, then since these authors condemn lying, especially in faith and morals, it is implausible they lied in saying 'thus says the Lord.' They were not deceived, as Paul's account of being caught up and hearing secret words (2 Cor 12) shows, since asserting what is doubtful is lying or close to it; such revelations show their intellects were moved to firm assent by a supernatural agent. Nor did they lie for gain, since they endured great sufferings for what they taught.
claims: The scriptural authors condemned lying and would not falsely claim divine speech.
They were not deceived, since firm assent to what nature cannot reveal requires a supernatural agent.
They did not lie for gain, since they suffered for their teaching.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e702.summary: The other horn: if the books are not by their attributed authors, then by parity any book's authorship could be denied, and it is unclear why only these were falsely ascribed. If the forgers were non-Christians, they would not have promoted a sect they opposed; if Christians, their law condemns lying. Nor could the books have become so authoritative and widespread unless genuinely by those authors.
claims: Denying the attributed authorship of Scripture would undermine all attributions of authorship.
Neither non-Christian nor Christian forgers are plausible.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e763.summary: Supporting authorities for the third way: Richard of St Victor (the faith was handed down by men of highest holiness); Augustine on Christ speaking through prophets, himself and apostles to establish canonical Scripture of eminent authority; and Augustine's letter to Jerome, that admitting even 'helpful lies' into Scripture would destroy its authority.
claims: Scripture's authority depends on its total freedom from falsehood.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e828.summary: Fourth way, diligence of the recipients: if one believed nothing contingent one had not seen, one could not believe the world existed before, that unvisited places exist, or who one's parents are, and political life would collapse. If one is to believe anyone about unseen contingents, it should above all be a whole respected community approving something with the greatest care. The scriptural canon is just this: Jews and Christians took more care over which books to receive as authentic than over any other writing, as containing what is necessary for salvation.
claims: Refusing all testimony about unseen contingents would destroy social life.
Testimony approved with great care by a whole respected community deserves the most belief.
The canon of Scripture was received with unmatched care by Jewish and Christian communities.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e899.summary: Augustinian support for the fourth way: the book of Enoch and other writings mentioned in Scripture were not received into the canon, which shows only works written by divine inspiration were admitted; and Israel never confused false prophets with true ones but recognized the concordant true prophets.
claims: Only works written under divine inspiration were admitted into the canon.
Israel carefully distinguished true from false prophets.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e953.summary: Fifth way, reasonableness of the content, first for morals: nothing is more reasonable than loving God above all as ultimate end and one's neighbor as oneself, on which the whole law depends, and the golden rule. From these as practical principles the other moral teachings of Scripture follow as honest and consonant with reason; precepts, counsels and sacraments all appear as an unfolding of the natural law written in hearts (Romans 2). Augustine adds that nothing shameful is proposed for imitation where God's precepts are taught.
claims: The love commandments and the golden rule are supremely reasonable practical principles.
Scripture's other moral teachings follow from them and are consonant with reason.
Scripture's moral teaching is an explication of the natural law.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e1043.summary: Reasonableness of the content of belief: nothing we believe about God implies imperfection; rather what we believe attests to divine perfection more than its opposite, as with the Trinity and Incarnation. Nor do we believe anything incredible, for then it would be incredible that the world believes it, yet we see that it does (Augustine). The honesty of Christian life is likewise attested.
claims: Nothing believed about God implies imperfection in God.
Articles such as the Trinity and Incarnation enhance rather than diminish divine perfection.
The world's actual belief shows the faith is not incredible.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e1096.summary: Sixth way, unreasonableness of each error, begun with pagans and Muslims. Pagan idolaters worship their own handiwork, in which the philosophers showed there is nothing divine. Against Islam, presented in harshly polemical terms, Scotus objects that it promises a bodily beatitude of food and sex, and cites Avicenna (Metaphysics IX.7), himself of that tradition, as holding a higher intellectual happiness, union with the first truth, to be more fitting and more desired by wise theologians.
claims: Idolatry is irrational, since artifacts have nothing divine.
A merely bodily beatitude is unworthy of human beings.
Avicenna himself placed intellectual happiness above bodily happiness.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e1166.summary: Against Judaism: the Jews reject the New Testament, which their own Old Testament promises (Jeremiah 31, as Hebrews shows); their ceremonies are empty without Christ; and their prophecies (Genesis 49, the sceptre not departing from Judah; Daniel 9) show that Christ has come and the New Testament he promulgated must be accepted as authentic.
claims: The Old Testament promises the New Covenant.
Old Testament prophecies show that the Messiah has come.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e1217.summary: Against the Manichaeans (abused polemically): they posit a first evil principle although every being as being is good, and they could have seen from the New Testament itself that the Old is authentic and approved.
claims: Every being, as being, is good, so there is no first evil principle.
The New Testament approves the Old.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e1237.summary: Against other heretics who build on single misunderstood words of Scripture: following Augustine (83 Questions), Christian-named error arises only from misunderstood Scripture, because readers do not compare a passage with its context or with other passages; heresies that arose from isolated reading were refuted by comparing texts that illuminate one another.
claims: Heresies within Christianity arise from misunderstood Scripture.
Context and comparison of passages correct such misreadings.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e1289.summary: Further against partial acceptance of Scripture: Augustine says he would not believe the Gospel except on the Catholic Church's authority; so it is unreasonable to accept some of the canon and not the rest, since the Church through which one receives the canon receives all of it equally. By contrast philosophical doctrines contain irrational elements, as Aristotle shows of others' constitutions in Politics II and as Aristotle's own views do in places (shown in the previous question).
claims: Belief in the canon rests on the Church's authority, which receives the whole canon equally.
Accepting part of the canon and rejecting part is therefore unreasonable.
Philosophical doctrines, Aristotle's included, contain irrational elements.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e1344.summary: Seventh way, stability of the Church. In its head: Augustine on the apostolic see's unbroken episcopal succession despite heretics, Gamaliel's counsel (Acts 5), and Christ's prayer that Peter's faith not fail (Luke 22). In its members: the common people of many nations believe and preach, and only God could lead a multitude prone to sin to keep a law contrary to flesh and blood. By contrast Judaism has not kept its vigor; and Islam, begun six centuries after Christ, is predicted to end soon, being much weakened around 1300.
claims: The Church's continuity in its head and members shows divine support.
Only God could bring a sinful multitude to keep a law contrary to the flesh.
Rival religions lack this stability.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e1499.summary: Eighth way, miracles: God cannot be a false witness; when invoked by a preacher of Scripture to show his doctrine true, God performed works proper to himself, miracles, and so testified to its truth. Richard of St Victor confirms: if this is error, we were deceived by God, since it was confirmed by signs only God could do.
claims: God cannot bear false witness.
Miracles are God's own works and serve as his testimony to the truth of what is preached.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e1541.summary: Two objections to the argument from miracles: that the miracles did not happen, or that they do not testify to truth since the Antichrist will work miracles. Against the first, Augustine's argument: if the miracles are disbelieved, it is itself a great miracle that the world came to believe without any miracles.
claims: If there were no miracles, the world's conversion would itself be a great miracle.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e1568.summary: Scotus urges attention to Augustine's argument: it would be no less incredible that a few obscure, uneducated men persuaded the world, the learned included, to believe so incredible a message without miracles. Few, poor and unlearned teachers converted many powerful and wise people to a law contrary to flesh and blood, as shown by converts who first opposed the faith, such as Paul, Augustine, Dionysius and Cyprian.
claims: The conversion of the learned and powerful by a few uneducated preachers is inexplicable without divine action.
Former opponents such as Paul and Augustine became teachers of the faith.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e1638.summary: Second reply to the claim that the miracles never happened: Augustine argues that one who denies all written testimony could equally deny that the gods care for mortals, and that those who credit magical or theurgic books have no reason to reject these. Third reply: some miracles, such as Sylvester's before Constantine (healing his leprosy and disputing with the Jews), are so famous that only the obstinate could deny them.
claims: Rejecting all written testimony to miracles is inconsistent with crediting other written testimony.
Some miracles are publicly attested beyond reasonable denial.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e1708.summary: Reply to the second objection (that miracles do not attest truth because the Antichrist will work them): if someone called as witness allows the usual sign of his testimony to be produced and does not contradict it, his silence is incompatible with perfect truthfulness. Miracles are God's sign as witness, so if he allowed demons to work them without disowning them he would not be perfectly truthful, which is impossible. In fact God foretold that the Antichrist's miracles would not attest truth (Matthew 24, 2 Thessalonians 2).
claims: Silence by a witness while his customary sign is falsely used is incompatible with perfect truthfulness.
God has explicitly disowned the Antichrist's miracles by foretelling them.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e1753.summary: A further reply to both objections: miracles worked by God differ from those of the devil. Augustine defines a miracle as anything difficult or unusual beyond the hope or power of the one who wonders; some only cause amazement, while others, like Christ's, win great grace and goodwill.
claims: Divine miracles are distinguishable from demonic ones by their character and effects.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e1784.summary: Against both objections: some Christian miracles admit no deception about their occurrence or divine source, namely Paul's rapture and the revelation of future contingents. One cannot be deceived in believing oneself to see the divine essence, a fortiori from the fact that one cannot be deceived in believing one understands a first principle, since seeing God differs more from any other understanding than grasping a principle differs from grasping a non-principle; and the intellect would know if it were not at rest. Since only God can beatify the soul even temporarily, Paul's vision was truly from God.
claims: No one can be deceived in believing they see the divine essence.
One cannot be deceived about understanding a first principle, and seeing God is even more distinct.
Only God can beatify a soul, even temporarily, so Paul's rapture was God's work.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e1904.summary: The second infallible miracle, prophecy of future contingents, is shown by many prophets in both Testaments. These two could even be used as tests against the Antichrist's false miracles: 'if you are God, let me see the divine essence and remember it with certainty,' or 'tell me what I will do or think at a given hour.' Christ points to this kind of evidence in John 5: believe the works.
claims: Prophecy of future contingents is a miracle proper to God.
The beatific vision and prophecy can serve as tests against false miracles.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e1949.summary: Two additional ways beyond the eight. Ninth, testimony of outsiders: Josephus on Christ's teaching and resurrection, the Sibylline prophecy, and the fact that heretics asked who is Catholic point to the true Catholics. Tenth, God does not fail those who seek salvation with their whole heart; many earnest seekers have converted to this faith, been strengthened in it the more fervently they sought, reformed their lives, and joyfully suffered torments for it, which suggests God approves this religion founded on Scripture and ordains it to salvation.
claims: Testimony from outside the faith supports its truth.
God does not abandon those who earnestly seek salvation.
The conversions and constancy of earnest seekers indicate divine approval of the Christian faith.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e2044.summary: Transition: having established against heretics that the canon's teaching is true, Scotus turns to the second issue, whether it is necessary and sufficient for the wayfarer to reach his end.
claims: The truth of canonical teaching has been established against heretics.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e2058.summary: Scotus's answer to the question proper: Scripture teaches what man's end is in particular, the vision and enjoyment of God, with its desirable circumstances (after the resurrection, by the immortal person in body and soul, without end). It also determines what is necessary for the end and that it suffices, namely the ten commandments (Matthew 19, Exodus 20), explained through various places in Scripture regarding what to believe, hope and do. It also teaches the properties of immaterial substances as far as is possible and useful. Measured against the three reasons used in the previous question, Scripture sufficiently contains the doctrine necessary for the wayfarer.
claims: Scripture teaches man's end in particular: the vision and enjoyment of God, in body and soul after the resurrection, without end.
Scripture teaches what is necessary for the end, the commandments, and that it suffices.
Scripture teaches about immaterial substances as far as is useful for the wayfarer.
Scripture sufficiently contains the doctrine necessary for the wayfarer.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e2115.summary: Reply to the first argument: the law of nature needed fewer things, which were passed down from fathers to sons by memory, and people then were better endowed naturally, so a little inspired teaching sufficed. Alternatively, the ordered progression of Scripture over time shows its divine teacher (Augustine, 83 Questions).
claims: Under the law of nature fewer truths were needed, transmitted orally, and people were better endowed naturally.
The ordered progression of Scripture reveals its divine author.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e2155.summary: Reply to the second argument: what is hidden under a literal sense is grasped more sweetly than what is stated outright, so the veiling in Old Testament figures of what the New makes explicit serves devotion; this covers the ceremonies. The histories provide examples that illustrate the law, and the whole course of Scripture shows God's ordered governance of humanity and all creation.
claims: Truths veiled in figures are more delightful to grasp and foster devotion.
Old Testament ceremonies prefigure New Testament realities.
Scriptural histories exemplify the law and reveal divine providence.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e2187.summary: Reply to the third argument, from Origen: no science states everything knowable, but only that from which the rest can sufficiently be drawn. Many necessary truths are not stated in Scripture but are virtually contained in it as conclusions in principles, and the work of commentators and doctors in drawing them out has been useful.
claims: No science expresses all its truths explicitly.
Necessary truths not explicit in Scripture are virtually contained in it as conclusions in principles.
The labor of theological interpreters is to draw these out.

jdso8u-d1e93-d1e2211.summary: Objection: even with all the doctors' teaching, many acts remain doubtful as to whether they are mortal sins. Reply: the way of salvation is not thereby doubtful, since one should guard against such acts as dangerous. Whoever, not caring for salvation, exposes himself to that danger sins mortally by so doing, even if the act in kind is not a mortal sin.
claims: Moral uncertainty does not make the way of salvation uncertain, because doubtful acts should be avoided.
Knowingly exposing oneself to the danger of mortal sin is itself a mortal sin.

jdso8u-d1e93.summary: Ordinatio I, Prologue part 2 (Wadding question 2): whether the supernatural knowledge the wayfarer needs is sufficiently handed down in Scripture. Against heretics who reject all or part of Scripture, Scotus first argues for its truth by eight rational 'ways' (prophecy, concord of the writers, their authority and veracity, the diligence of the receiving communities, the reasonableness of its moral and doctrinal content, the unreasonableness of rival errors, the stability of the Church, and miracles), adding outsiders' testimony and the constancy of earnest seekers. The treatment of rival religions is sharply polemical. He then answers that Scripture is necessary and sufficient: it teaches man's particular end (vision and enjoyment of God in body and soul after the resurrection), what is necessary to attain it (the commandments, unfolded for belief, hope and action), and what is useful about immaterial substances. The objections are answered by appeal to the reduced needs under the law of nature, the devotional value of figures and the providential lessons of history, and the virtual containment of necessary truths in Scripture, with moral doubt resolved by avoiding danger.
claims: The truth of Scripture can be rationally supported by multiple motives of credibility.
Scripture sufficiently contains the supernatural doctrine necessary for the wayfarer.
Necessary truths not explicit in Scripture are virtually contained in it and drawn out by interpreters.
Moral uncertainty does not render the way of salvation uncertain.
